explanations.explanation: Proud is it, baker. Paul says, "And you are proud!" (1 Corinthians 5:2). That's like scorching a whole batch and then taking a bow. Then he says what they should have felt instead, which is grief.
It's a fair guess, friend, since you'd expect a church to be shocked. But Paul doesn't say shocked. He says, "And you are proud!" (1 Corinthians 5:2). Grief is what he says they should have felt.

Afraid is a reasonable guess, but Paul never mentions fear here. What he says is, "And you are proud!" (1 Corinthians 5:2). That's the word, so hold onto it. Then he says what they should have felt, which is grief.

Yes, fellowship. Paul asks if they shouldn't have "…removed from your fellowship the man who did this?" (1 Corinthians 5:2). It's about the circle of the church, the people gathered together. He's talking about who stays in that circle.
City is a big jump, friend. Paul doesn't say a word about a city. He talks about removing the man from their fellowship (1 Corinthians 5:2). That's the group of believers they share life with.
Synagogue sounds churchy, but Paul doesn't use it here. He says the man should have been removed from their fellowship (1 Corinthians 5:2). The word is about the believers together, not a building.

Close, but Paul isn't holding off. He says he has "…already pronounced judgment on the one who did this, just as if I were present." (1 Corinthians 5:3). He's absent in body but present in spirit, as he puts it. So the judgment is already made.

That's right. Paul says, "…I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did this, just as if I were present." (1 Corinthians 5:3). He's absent in body but present in spirit, as he puts it. No waiting around for him.

Saved is it. Paul says the man is handed over "…so that his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord." (1 Corinthians 5:5). That's the reason Paul gives, and it's heavy, but it's not hopeless. I think that's worth sitting with for a second.
Rewarded sounds nice, but it isn't Paul's word. He says the man is handed over "…so that his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord." (1 Corinthians 5:5). Saved is the word on the page.

Silenced is a sharp guess, friend, but Paul doesn't say it. He says the man is handed over "…so that his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord." (1 Corinthians 5:5). The goal Paul names is his spirit being saved.
True! Paul asks, "Do you not know that a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough?" (1 Corinthians 5:6). Leaven doesn't stay in one corner. It works through the whole batch.

Not this time. Paul asks, "Do you not know that a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough?" (1 Corinthians 5:6). He's saying a little leaven reaches the whole batch. It doesn't stay in one spot.
Passover is right. Paul writes, "For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed." (1 Corinthians 5:7). He's the lamb in the picture. And that's a line I never get tired of hearing.

Pentecost is a good feast name, but it isn't the one Paul uses here. He writes, "For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed." (1 Corinthians 5:7). Passover is the one he names. Easy to mix up when feasts all start sounding like parties.

Tabernacles is a feast name too, friend, but it isn't the one Paul uses. He writes, "For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed." (1 Corinthians 5:7). Just before that, he tells them to get rid of the old leaven so they can be a new unleavened batch. Then he adds that line about Christ, the Passover lamb.

Yes! Paul says to keep the feast with "…the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth." (1 Corinthians 5:8). That's the opposite of the malice and wickedness in the old bread. Sincerity and truth are what he says belong at this feast.

Those are good things, but they're not what Paul says here. He says the bread is "…the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth." (1 Corinthians 5:8). Fasting and prayer aren't in this verse. Sincerity and truth are.
Rest and quiet sound lovely, friend, but Paul doesn't say that. He says the bread is "…the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth." (1 Corinthians 5:8). Those are the two words to remember.

Not quite, friend. Paul says he was not including the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters (1 Corinthians 5:10). If he had meant them all, he says, "…you would have to leave this world." So he wasn't telling them to avoid everyone out there.

That's right, friend. Paul says he didn't mean the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters (1 Corinthians 5:10). Staying away from all of them would mean leaving this world, and he says so himself. So what he's asking of them is narrower than that.

explanations.answer: Anyone who claims to be a brother but lives that way
explanations.explanation: That's it. Paul writes, "But now I am writing you not to associate with anyone who claims to be a brother but is sexually immoral or greedy, an idolater or a verbal abuser, a drunkard or a swindler." (1 Corinthians 5:11). He's speaking about someone who claims to be a brother. Paul spells it out plainly.

explanations.answer: Anyone who teaches in the church but lives that way
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say teacher anywhere in this verse. He says, "…anyone who claims to be a brother…" and lives that way (1 Corinthians 5:11). The word is brother, not teacher. That's the line he draws.

explanations.answer: Anyone who visits the church once but lives that way
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Paul says, "…anyone who claims to be a brother…" and lives that way (1 Corinthians 5:11). What marks the person is that claim together with the conduct he lists. How often someone visits isn't what Paul mentions.

Not this time, friend. Paul says not to associate with such a man, and then adds, "With such a man do not even eat." (1 Corinthians 5:11). The list includes the greedy, drunkards and swindlers. So sharing a meal isn't left open.
Correct. Paul says, "With such a man do not even eat." (1 Corinthians 5:11). He's speaking of anyone who claims to be a brother but is greedy, a drunkard or a swindler. So no sharing meals with him.

True. Paul says, "God will judge those outside." (1 Corinthians 5:13). Just before that, he asks what business it is of his to judge those outside the church (1 Corinthians 5:12). So outside judging is left to God.

Not quite, friend. Paul says, "God will judge those outside." (1 Corinthians 5:13). He'd just asked what business it is of his to judge those outside the church (1 Corinthians 5:12). So that judging is God's.
Yes. Paul ends with a quote: "Expel the wicked man from among you." (1 Corinthians 5:13). It's the closing line of the chapter. That's a heavy one, friend, but it's what the text says.

explanations.answer: Pray for him day and night
explanations.explanation: Prayer is a good thing, but it isn't Paul's closing command here. He ends with, "Expel the wicked man from among you." (1 Corinthians 5:13). That's the line the chapter finishes on.

explanations.answer: Send him to Paul at once
explanations.explanation: Paul isn't asking for the man to be sent to him. He says he's absent in body (1 Corinthians 5:3). His closing command is, "Expel the wicked man from among you." (1 Corinthians 5:13). The church is the one to act.
